Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

SimpleHelp bug lets hackers create rogue remote support accounts

BleepingComputer
2026-06-15 8 use cases 1 technique 6 kill-chain phases detected

A vulnerability in the SimpleHelp remote management software allows unauthenticated attackers to create privileged technician accounts on servers using the OpenID Connect (OIDC) authentication protocol. [...]

CVEsCVE-2026-48558
ATT&CKT1190
Domainshorizon3.ai

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Internet-exposed SimpleHelp servers vulnerable to CVE-2026-48558 · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Rogue SimpleHelp Technician account created via OIDC bypass (CVE-2026-48558) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — SimpleHelp bug lets hackers create rogue remote support accounts
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] SimpleHelp 'Remote Access.exe' spawning script interpreters on managed endpoints · [LLM] Newly created SimpleHelp Technician immediately exercises privileged actions
Rogue SimpleHelp Technician account created via OIDC bypass (CVE-2026-48558) AIInstallation High
Detects new Technician account registrations/logons in the SimpleHelp server audit log forwarded as syslog. Targets the exact persistence vector from CVE-2026-48558 where forged OIDC identity assertions register an attacker-controlled privileged Technician without MFA. Rationale: Article explicitly names /opt/SimpleHelp/logs/server.log as the audit trail that records 'technician registrations, email addresses, and configuration changes performed by rogue accounts'. Cross-checked with Horizon3.ai disclosure which calls out IoC review focused on 'new authenticated technician users with unknown or suspicious names and/or email addresses' and confirms OIDC is the bypassed code path. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/disclosures/cve-2026-48558-simplehelp-authentication-bypass-iocs/ • https://www.securityweek.com/vulnerabilities-in-simplehelp-remote-access-software-may-lead-to-system-compromise/
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1078.004 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new MSP technician onboarded via OIDC SSO and provisioned just-in-time
  • IT bulk-imports staff into a new SimpleHelp Technician Group on first OIDC rollout
  • Test/QA Technician accounts spun up for SimpleHelp version 5.5.16 upgrade verification
  • Existing technician's UPN changes after a HR rename (creates 'new' OIDC identity)
Suppression filter
| where not (NewUser in ("", "system") or Email endswith "@yourcorp.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the full server.log block for the new Technician: capture username, email domain, OIDC subject claim, source IP, Technician Group joined, and whether 'Allow group authenticated logins' is enabled on that group; cross-check the username/email against HR/IdP directory. 2) Contain — if the user is not in the IdP directory or the source IP is foreign, immediately disable the Technician account in SimpleHelp, revoke any active sessions, IP-allowlist Technician logins, and verify the server is on 5.5.16 / 6.0RC2 (patch CVE-2026-48558). 3) Hunt — pivot on the same source IP/UA across server.log for prior OIDC probes; review session history for managed-endpoint remote-control or script-execution actions launched by the rogue Technician within the next 24h (feeds UC4).
let LookbackDays = 7d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ProcessName has "SimpleHelp" or SyslogMessage has "SimpleHelp"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("Technician", "technician")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("created", "registered", "added", "OIDC login", "new technician")
| extend NewUser = extract(@"(?i)technician[^\w]+([\w._-]+@?[\w._-]*)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend Email = extract(@"([\w._%+-]+@[\w.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,})", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend OidcFlag = iff(SyslogMessage has "OIDC" or SyslogMessage has "openid", "oidc", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, OidcFlag, NewUser, Email, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:simplehelp (@message:*Technician* OR @message:*technician*) (@message:*created* OR @message:*registered* OR @message:*added* OR @message:*"OIDC login"*) (@message:*OIDC* OR @message:*openid*)
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(Authentication.src) as src values(Authentication.user) as user values(Authentication.signature) as signature from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="SimpleHelp" (Authentication.signature IN ("TechnicianCreated","TechnicianRegistered","OIDCLogin","technician_added") OR Authentication.action="success") Authentication.authentication_method="OIDC" by Authentication.user Authentication.src Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where firstSeen >= relative_time(now(),"-7d") | eval suspicious=if(match(user, "(?i)(test|admin[0-9]+|temp|qa|root|svc)") OR len(user)<4 OR match(user,"^[a-z0-9]{8,}$"),1,0)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstSeen max(_time) as lastSeen values(Authentication.src) as src values(Authentication.user) as user values(Authentication.signature) as signature from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.app="SimpleHelp" (Authentication.signature IN ("TechnicianCreated","TechnicianRegistered","OIDCLogin","technician_added") OR Authentication.action="success") Authentication.authentication_method="OIDC" by Authentication.user Authentication.src Authentication.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where firstSeen >= relative_time(now(),"-7d") | eval suspicious=if(match(user, "(?i)(test|admin[0-9]+|temp|qa|root|svc)") OR len(user)<4 OR match(user,"^[a-z0-9]{8,}$"),1,0)
SimpleHelp 'Remote Access.exe' spawning script interpreters on managed endpoints AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-exploitation pivot from CVE-2026-48558: a rogue Technician using SimpleHelp's 'execute scripts' capability against managed endpoints. Looks for the SimpleHelp customer-client binary spawning shells or LOLBin script interpreters, which is the only on-endpoint signal an attacker leaves when abusing the platform. Rationale: Article describes the SimpleHelp Technician role as 'remoting into managed endpoints, executing scripts, and more' — the only on-endpoint footprint of that abuse is the customer-client binary spawning shells. Binary name 'Remote Access.exe' (vendor 'SimpleHelp LTD') corroborated by Arctic Wolf's prior SimpleHelp campaign write-up — kept generic on installation path because SimpleHelp installs vary per deployment. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/arctic-wolf-observes-campaign-exploiting-simplehelp-rmm-software-for-initial-access/ • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/disclosures/cve-2026-48558-simplehelp-authentication-bypass-iocs/
ATT&CKT1219 T1059 T1072
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Help-desk technician runs a legitimate cmd/PowerShell command during a support call
  • MSP-pushed scheduled scripts (patch installers, log collectors) launched via SimpleHelp remote session
  • SimpleHelp's built-in 'Tools' menu running diagnostic commands (ipconfig, systeminfo)
  • Endpoint inventory script invoked by IT during fleet audit
  • Vendor-supplied update wrapped as a script and pushed through SimpleHelp
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("\\Get-ComputerInfo", "\\ipconfig", "systeminfo", "\\WindowsUpdate")) and not (AccountName in~ ("known-helpdesk-svc"))
Response runbook
1) Triage — pull the full child command line, SHA256, and the Technician name driving the SimpleHelp session from server.log within ±2 min of the spawn; check if the Technician is a known-good IdP user. 2) Contain — if the Technician is unknown / brand-new / has a suspicious email domain, kill the SimpleHelp session, isolate the affected endpoint via MDE, disable the Technician account on the SimpleHelp server, and rotate any creds typed during the session. 3) Hunt — pivot on the Technician's identity across server.log for every other endpoint they touched in the last 14d; sweep those endpoints for the same parent→child pattern, plus newly written persistence artifacts (services, Run keys, scheduled tasks) attributed to 'Remote Access.exe'.
let Lookback = 7d;
let Lolbins = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "Remote Access.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("SimpleHelp", "SimpleHelp LTD") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "SimpleHelp"
| where FileName in~ (Lolbins)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          ChildSHA256 = SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 7d;
let Lolbins = dynamic(["cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\Remote Access.exe" or ActingProcessName =~ "Remote Access.exe"
| where (ActingProcessFileCompany has_any ("SimpleHelp", "SimpleHelp LTD")) or ActingProcessName has "SimpleHelp"
| extend ChildExe = tostring(split(TargetProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where tolower(ChildExe) in (Lolbins)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine,
          TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SimpleHelp Remote Access Spawning Shell or LOLBin Script Interpreter
id: 6a3f1f0a-9b1e-4d2d-8e7f-9c2b8b1f4d22
description: Detects the SimpleHelp customer-client process ('Remote Access.exe', SimpleHelp LTD) spawning shells or LOLBin script interpreters. After CVE-2026-48558, rogue OIDC-registered Technicians can drive arbitrary script execution on managed endpoints via this exact chain.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/simplehelp-bug-lets-hackers-create-rogue-remote-support-accounts/
  - https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/disclosures/cve-2026-48558-simplehelp-authentication-bypass-iocs/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/15
tags:
  - attack.t1219
  - attack.t1059
  - attack.t1072
  - attack.execution
  - attack.lateral_movement
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\Remote Access.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'

| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|wscript|cscript|mshta|rundll32|regsvr32|bitsadmin|certutil|curl|wget)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentImageFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, UserName], function=count())
| count > 0

Asset-surface hunt for SimpleHelp servers running 5.5.15 or older / 6.0 pre-release that are reachable from the internet — the entire prerequisite for CVE-2026-48558 exploitation. Rationale: Article gives the exact patched versions (5.5.16, 6.0RC2 released June 9 2026) and prerequisite (internet-exposed server with OIDC). Detection joins Defender TVM CveId lookup against DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing so SOC can prioritise the ~14,000-server exposure cited by Horizon3.ai's Shodan analysis. Image [3] in the article also visually confirms a rogue Technician landed on a real server console. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/disclosures/cve-2026-48558-simplehelp-authentication-bypass-iocs/ • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-48558

Newly created SimpleHelp Technician immediately exercises privileged actions AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates a brand-new Technician registration in SimpleHelp server.log with privileged actions (remote-session start, script execution, group/role change) by that same account within minutes. The compressed timeline is the signature of CVE-2026-48558 abuse — legitimate onboarding flows have a HR/training gap. Rationale: Article emphasises that the rogue Technician is *immediately* usable for 'remoting into managed endpoints, executing scripts'. Kill-chain block phase 4 detection hint: 'Newly created Technician accounts immediately exercising privileged actions ... shortly after first login'. The 15-minute window keeps onboarding-with-immediate-use FPs but eliminates legitimate flows where HR creates the account hours before first use. Cross-checked against: • https://horizon3.ai/attack-research/disclosures/cve-2026-48558-simplehelp-authentication-bypass-iocs/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSP runbook that provisions a Technician and immediately runs a smoke-test remote session

Suppression filter
| where DelaySec >= 5
Response runbook
1) Triage — capture the new Technician's username, email, OIDC sub claim, source IP, and the exact privileged action taken (which managed endpoint did they hit, which script ran). 2) Contain — disable the Technician account in SimpleHelp, kill any in-flight remote sessions to the targeted endpoints, isolate those endpoints via MDE, and snapshot for forensics; if the server is still on a vulnerable version, patch to 5.5.16 / 6.0RC2 immediately. 3) Hunt — for the source IP and OIDC sub claim, enumerate all SimpleHelp authentications and every endpoint the rogue Technician interacted with; on each endpoint, run UC2 retro-active and inspect created services, scheduled tasks, and outbound C2 connections from 'Remote Access.exe' or its children.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let WindowMinutes = 15m;
let Creations = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ProcessName has "SimpleHelp" or SyslogMessage has "SimpleHelp"
    | where SyslogMessage matches regex @"(?i)technician.*?(created|registered|added)"
    | extend NewUser = extract(@"(?i)technician[^\w]+([\w._-]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(NewUser)
    | project CreateTime = TimeGenerated, NewUser, Computer, CreationMsg = SyslogMessage;
let PrivActions = Syslog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where ProcessName has "SimpleHelp" or SyslogMessage has "SimpleHelp"
    | where SyslogMessage has_any ("remote session", "script", "group modified", "configuration changed", "role", "privilege")
    | extend ActorUser = extract(@"(?i)(?:user|technician|by)[^\w]+([\w._-]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
    | where isnotempty(ActorUser)
    | project ActionTime = TimeGenerated, ActorUser, Computer, ActionMsg = SyslogMessage;
Creations
| join kind=inner (PrivActions) on $left.NewUser == $right.ActorUser
| where ActionTime between (CreateTime .. CreateTime + WindowMinutes)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', ActionTime, CreateTime)
| project CreateTime, ActionTime, DelaySec, NewUser, Computer, CreationMsg, ActionMsg
| order by ActionTime desc

Vitest Browser Mode API bound to all interfaces (CVE-2026-53633 false-sense-of-security config) AIExploitation High
Hunts for Node/pnpm/npm/npx/yarn launching Vitest with the browser-mode API explicitly bound to 0.0.0.0. Per the advisory, this is the precondition that turns the CDP bridge into a network-reachable RCE primitive, and `allowWrite:false`/`allowExec:false` do NOT mitigate it. Rationale: Pivots on the exact misconfiguration the GHSA advisory calls out as the network-exposure pre-req: `--browser.api.host=0.0.0.0` (or YAML equivalent) combined with a Vitest/vite-plus invocation. The optional WriteExecHardened column flags the precise false-sense-of-security case (CDP bypass active despite allowWrite/allowExec=false). Cross-checked GitHub Security Advisory and Vitest docs confirming 63315/0.0.0.0 binding semantics. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://vitest.dev/config/browser/api • https://securityonline.info/vitest-remote-code-execution-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer intentionally testing on a phone/tablet on the same LAN binds to 0.0.0.0 deliberately
  • CI runner in a private subnet binds 0.0.0.0 because the build agent and browser run on separate containers
  • Devcontainer / WSL2 setup binding 0.0.0.0 so host browser can reach the in-VM Vitest
  • Documentation copy-paste that left --host=0.0.0.0 in an npm script
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("code.exe","devenv.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("127.0.0.1","localhost"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: confirm host is a developer workstation/CI runner. Capture parent process tree — was the command typed by the user (cmd.exe/pwsh.exe parent) or invoked from a package.json script (parent=npm-cli/pnpm)? Check if the Vitest server is still listening: `netstat -ano | findstr 63315`. 2. CONTAIN: if still running, kill the node PID and rotate the project's Vitest API token; quarantine the workstation if any inbound connection to 63315 from a non-loopback IP exists in the last 7d (run UC #2). 3. HUNT: pivot on user — search DeviceFileEvents for any modifications to vite.config.ts/vitest.config.ts in the last 14d initiated by a browser binary (UC #3), and DeviceProcessEvents for node.exe spawned from a browser-touched config (UC #4). Patch @vitest/browser to a non-vulnerable version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","pnpm.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe","node")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","pnpm.exe","npm.exe","npx.exe","yarn.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("vitest","@vitest/browser","vite-plus")

title: Vitest Browser Mode API Bound to All Interfaces (CVE-2026-53633)
id: 4e1b8d20-7c63-4b9f-9e0a-1f2a3b4c5d6e
description: Detects Node-based Vitest invocations that bind the Browser Mode API to 0.0.0.0, exposing the CDP-capable WebSocket RPC bridge to the network. Per GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm the allowWrite/allowExec flags do NOT gate CDP, so this configuration is remotely exploitable for RCE.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
  - https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm

Inbound non-loopback connection to Vitest Browser Mode API port 63315 AIDelivery High
Detects a remote IP connecting to TCP/63315 (Vitest's default browser API/WebSocket port) on a workstation or CI host. Per the advisory, an active session plus a non-loopback client equals exploitability — attacker only needs the token exposed at `/__vitest_test__/`. Rationale: Port 63315 is Vitest's documented default for the browser API (corroborated via Vitest docs and the issue #9035 discussion). Inbound to that port from anything other than loopback on a workstation is the article's exact remote-exploit precondition. Initiating-process filter narrows to Vitest/browser listeners to suppress unrelated services that may transiently bind a high port. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://vitest.dev/config/browser/api • https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/issues/9035
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer on a corporate LAN reaching their own workstation's dev server from a second device
  • CI agent / container in same private subnet making a legitimate health-check probe
  • Internal vulnerability scanner sweeping ephemeral high ports
  • Service collision — another local service transiently bound to 63315 (rare but possible on ephemeral-port allocation)
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP startswith "10." or RemoteIP startswith "192.168." or RemoteIP startswith "172.16." or RemoteIP startswith "172.17." or RemoteIP startswith "172.18." or RemoteIP startswith "172.19." or RemoteIP startswith "172.2" or RemoteIP startswith "172.30." or RemoteIP startswith "172.31.") or RemoteIP in (dynamic(["<known-dev-LAN-CIDRs>"]))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: confirm the destination host is running Vitest browser-mode (cross-check with UC #1). Identify the remote IP — is it RFC1918 (likely internal dev), VPN exit, or public? Geolocate public IPs. 2. CONTAIN: if remote IP is unknown/public, isolate the workstation, kill the node PID, and rotate any project secrets exposed on disk (VITEST_API_TOKEN, .env). Block 63315 inbound at the host firewall going forward. 3. HUNT: pivot on the source IP — search for other Vitest hosts contacted from same IP. Check DeviceFileEvents on the target host for any vite.config.* modifications by browser binaries within 5 minutes of the connection (UC #3). Search proxy logs for fetches to `/__vitest_test__/` or `/__vitest_browser_api__` from that IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("InboundConnectionAccepted","ListeningConnectionCreated")
| where LocalPort == 63315
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType !in ("Loopback")
| where RemoteIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1","0.0.0.0")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","chrome.exe","chromium.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","headless_shell.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("vitest","@vitest/browser","vite-plus")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteIPType, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber == 63315
| where NetworkDirection in~ ("Inbound","Listen")
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1","::1","0.0.0.0")
| where not (ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr) and SrcIpAddr == DstIpAddr)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcPortNumber, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, EventProduct, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects a non-loopback inbound TCP connection to port 63315, the default Vitest Browser Mode API/WebSocket port. With an active Vitest browser session, this is the network preconditions for CDP-based config overwrite RCE.

Browser binary overwrites vite.config.* / vitest.config.* (CVE-2026-53633 CDP exploit) AIInstallation High
Detects a Chromium/Edge/Firefox binary writing a vite or vitest config file. Browsers do not normally touch project config; per the advisory, this is the exact filesystem side-effect of the CDP `Page.setDownloadBehavior` + `Runtime.evaluate` chain that lands attacker-controlled Node code via Vitest's config-reload behaviour. Rationale: Direct fingerprint of the CDP-driven exploit per the advisory's reproduction steps. Browser processes have no legitimate reason to create or modify Vite/Vitest configuration files; the only ways this happens are (a) this exploit, or (b) a browser-based IDE that's unusual on a dev workstation. The .crdownload / .part / .tmp variants catch the Chromium download-temp filename it briefly uses before rename. Includes the Playwright Chromium binary names (headless_shell.exe, 'Google Chrome for Testing.exe') called out in the article's reproduction. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
ATT&CKT1546 T1574 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using a Chromium-based VS Code-for-Web / GitHub Codespaces browser tab that writes through the browser sandbox (rare)
  • User dragging a vite.config.ts from another tab into Downloads, then renaming into project (would show download-from-URL with referrer)
  • Browser-based file-manager (e.g. Files.app, Mega) syncing a project folder including a config file
  • Security tooling that lives in-browser writing to local filesystem (e.g. Chrome extensions with FileSystem API)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "msedge.exe" and FolderPath has_any ("\\Downloads\\","\\Desktop\\") and isnotempty(FileOriginUrl) and FileOriginUrl !contains "localhost" and FileOriginUrl !contains "127.0.0.1")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: pull the file contents — `Get-Content` on the modified vite.config.*; look for `child_process`, `require('child_process')`, `import('child_process')`, `fs.writeFileSync`, `process.env`, base64 blobs, or callbacks to attacker infra. Capture FileOriginUrl/FileOriginIP from the same event — that is your C2 indicator. Pull DeviceNetworkEvents for inbound 63315 within 5 minutes preceding (UC #2). 2. CONTAIN: isolate the host, kill node and the browser process tree, revert the config file from git (`git checkout -- vite.config.ts`), rotate any secrets in .env / package.json scripts. Block the FileOriginIP at egress. 3. HUNT: pivot on FileOriginUrl across the fleet (DeviceNetworkEvents). Search DeviceProcessEvents for node.exe spawned within 30s of the file write across all hosts (UC #4) — that's the RCE going off. Across CI: check pipeline run history for any Vitest job that consumed an altered config.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName in~ (
    "vite.config.ts","vite.config.js","vite.config.mjs","vite.config.cjs","vite.config.mts","vite.config.cts",
    "vitest.config.ts","vitest.config.js","vitest.config.mjs","vitest.config.cjs","vitest.config.mts","vitest.config.cts")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^v(it)?est?\.config\.[mc]?[jt]s$"
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)^v(it)?est?\.config\.(ts|js|mjs|cjs|mts|cts)\.(crdownload|part|tmp|download)$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","chromium.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","headless_shell.exe","Google Chrome for Testing.exe","opera.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)(chromium|chrome|headless_shell)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginIP, FileOriginReferrerUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessParentId, RequestSourceIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileCreate","FileWrite")
| where TargetFileName in~ (
    "vite.config.ts","vite.config.js","vite.config.mjs","vite.config.cjs","vite.config.mts","vite.config.cts",
    "vitest.config.ts","vitest.config.js","vitest.config.mjs","vitest.config.cjs","vitest.config.mts","vitest.config.cts")
   or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^v(it)?est?\.config\.(ts|js|mjs|cjs|mts|cts)(\.(crdownload|part|tmp))?$"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(chrome|chromium|msedge|firefox|brave|headless_shell|opera)\.exe$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Browser Process Overwriting Vite/Vitest Config File (CVE-2026-53633)
id: 7a3d8e42-b91f-4c5d-a8e0-3f4051627384
description: Detects a Chromium/Edge/Firefox/Brave binary creating or modifying vite.config.* or vitest.config.* files. Per GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm this is the direct filesystem side-effect of the CDP Page.setDownloadBehavior + Runtime.evaluate exploit chain that lands attacker-controlled Node.js in the project's config and triggers RCE on Vitest's auto-reload.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
  - https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
author: Detection Pipeline

      - '\chromium.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '\headless_shell.exe'

      - '\vite.config.ts'

      - '\vite.config.mts'

falsepositives:
  - Developer manually saving a config file via a browser-based IDE that writes through the browser process (very rare; most browser IDEs use a backend service)
level: critical
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) @EventID:11 @Image:(*\chrome.exe OR *\Chrome.exe OR *\chromium.exe OR *\Chromium.exe OR *\msedge.exe OR *\MsEdge.exe OR *\firefox.exe OR *\Firefox.exe OR *\brave.exe OR *\headless_shell.exe OR *\Google Chrome for Testing.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\vite.config.ts OR *\vite.config.js OR *\vite.config.mjs OR *\vite.config.cjs OR *\vite.config.mts OR *\vite.config.cts OR *\vitest.config.ts OR *\vitest.config.js OR *\vitest.config.mjs OR *\vitest.config.cjs OR *\vitest.config.mts OR *\vitest.config.cts)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|chromium|msedge|firefox|brave|headless_shell|opera)\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\v(it)?est?\\.config\\.(ts|js|mjs|cjs|mts|cts)(\\.(crdownload|part|tmp))?$", field=TargetFileName, flags="i")

Vitest config overwrite followed by rapid node.exe respawn (CVE-2026-53633 RCE trigger) AIExploitation High
Correlates the file-write side of the exploit (UC #3) with Vitest's reload behaviour — a node.exe running `vitest` re-executes within seconds of the config being modified, which is where the attacker-controlled JS actually runs. The delay-seconds field makes the chain pop visually for triage. Rationale: Captures the full RCE chain end-to-end: the browser-driven config overwrite from UC #3 plus Vitest's `watch`-mode config reload re-spawning Node within seconds, which is when the attacker code actually runs. DelaySec gives the analyst an immediate triage signal — anything sub-15s with a browser writer is the textbook GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm exploit timing. Sigma omitted: this is a time-window correlation across two tables, not single-event-shape. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm
ATT&CKT1546 T1574 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer manually editing the config (would not have a browser-process writer — UC #3 filter already gates this)
  • Vitest watch mode reload after a legitimate save through a backend (writer process would be the editor, not chrome.exe)
  • CI runner reloading after a checked-in config update (parent process would be git/CI agent, not browser)
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: this is a high-confidence exploit chain — assume compromise. Grab the config file contents BEFORE the host reboots, capture the FileOriginUrl/OriginIP from UC #3, capture the full node.exe command line and child process tree (DeviceProcessEvents pivoting on NodeSpawnTime + 5min). 2. CONTAIN: isolate the host immediately, kill the node process tree, revert vite.config.* from git, rotate developer credentials/SSH/git tokens that were available to the node process (`process.env`), revoke any AWS/cloud creds with the workstation IAM role. Block the OriginIP at egress. 3. HUNT: across the fleet — pivot OriginUrl and OriginIP against DeviceNetworkEvents (other hosts attacker reached); pivot the SHA256 of any binary the node child spawned; check DeviceFileEvents for any new files (especially `~/.ssh/*`, `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.npmrc`) written in the 10 minutes after NodeSpawnTime. Open IR ticket — likely full workstation rebuild.
let Window = 30s;
let ConfigWrites =
    DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
    | where FileName in~ ("vite.config.ts","vite.config.js","vite.config.mjs","vite.config.cjs","vite.config.mts","vite.config.cts",
                          "vitest.config.ts","vitest.config.js","vitest.config.mjs","vitest.config.cjs","vitest.config.mts","vitest.config.cts")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)\\(chrome|chromium|msedge|firefox|brave|headless_shell|opera)\.exe$"
    | project ConfigWriteTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, ConfigFolder=FolderPath, ConfigFile=FileName,
              WriterProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName, OriginUrl=FileOriginUrl, OriginIP=FileOriginIP;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("vitest","vite","@vitest/browser")
| join kind=inner ConfigWrites on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (ConfigWriteTime .. ConfigWriteTime + Window)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ConfigWriteTime)
| project ConfigWriteTime, NodeSpawnTime=Timestamp, DelaySec, DeviceName, AccountName, ConfigFolder, ConfigFile, WriterProcess, OriginUrl, OriginIP, NodeCmd=ProcessCommandLine, NodeParent=InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ConfigWriteTime desc
let Window = 30s;
let ConfigWrites =
    ImFileEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventType in~ ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed","FileCreate","FileWrite")
    | where TargetFileName in~ ("vite.config.ts","vite.config.js","vite.config.mjs","vite.config.cjs",
                                "vitest.config.ts","vitest.config.js","vitest.config.mjs","vitest.config.cjs")
    | where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\(chrome|chromium|msedge|firefox|brave|headless_shell)\.exe$"
    | project ConfigWriteTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ConfigFile=TargetFileName, ConfigPath=TargetFilePath, WriterProcess=ActingProcessName;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

Inbound to Vitest API followed by browser-process file write into Vitest project root AIDelivery Medium
Full kill-chain correlation: a non-loopback inbound connection to port 63315 followed within minutes by a browser binary writing a file into a directory that contains an existing vite/vitest config or package.json. Catches the CDP `Page.setDownloadBehavior` + `Runtime.evaluate` chain even when the attacker drops something other than `vite.config.ts` (alternate config names, fixture files, payload precursors). Rationale: Covers the article's reproduction sequence end-to-end (step 3 connect to WS API → step 5 Runtime.evaluate triggers a browser-side download into project root) without locking the file-name pattern to vite.config.* — picks up attacker variants that drop alternate payloads (package.json, lib/index.js, src/setup.ts) into a project root. RemoteIP attribution is the bonus: file-only detections (UC #3) lose the attacker IP that this correlation preserves. Sigma omitted: cross-table time-window correlation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/security/advisories/GHSA-g8mr-85jm-7xhm • https://vitest.dev/config/browser/api
ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Cross-device dev testing where the second device legitimately uploads test fixtures via the Vitest API
  • Internal CI agent fetching artefacts during a build that happens to write into the project root
  • Browser-based collaborative editor with file-sync running against a project folder
  • Legitimate Vitest snapshot/fixture uploads via WebSocket annotation API (article notes Vitest writes annotation attachments via the same channel)
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP in (dynamic(["<known-dev-LAN-CIDRs>","<CI-agent-IPs>"])))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: cross-check the RemoteIP against known dev devices and VPN exits. Inspect the WrittenFile contents — `child_process`, base64, `process.env`, or unusual imports are the red flags. Pull DeviceProcessEvents for any node.exe spawn within 30s of WriteTime (chains into UC #4). 2. CONTAIN: if RemoteIP is unknown/public, isolate the workstation, kill node and browser processes, revert all files written by the browser process in the project root over the last 24h, rotate workstation credentials. Block the RemoteIP at egress. 3. HUNT: pivot RemoteIP across the entire fleet — any other inbound 63315 hits? Pull proxy/IIS logs for any request to `/__vitest_test__/` or `/__vitest_browser_api__` from that IP. Check git history for any unauthorized commits attributed to this workstation in the same window.

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

INFINITERED REDCap backdoor SHA256 file write on web server AIInstallation Medium
Detects file-write events on REDCap servers whose SHA256 matches GTIG-published INFINITERED hashes. INFINITERED trojanizes REDCap's own PHP/system files and reinjects on upgrade, so any disk write of these hashes by the web-server process indicates active UNC6508 compromise. Rationale: Pivots on the seven GTIG-published INFINITERED SHA256s named as IOCs for UNC6508 in the article. Hash-based detection is unaffected by REDCap version since INFINITERED reinjects on upgrade. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1554
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AV/EDR pre-staged scan repository writing the sample for analysis
  • DFIR responder copying retrieved samples to evidence share
  • Honeypot or canary REDCap instance intentionally storing known-bad
  • Security researcher running INFINITERED in an isolated lab
  • Threat-intel platform syncing hash artifacts to disk
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","CSFalconService.exe")
| where FolderPath !contains "\\Quarantine\\"
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify host role (is this a REDCap web server?) and confirm the writing process is the web stack (php-fpm, httpd, w3wp). Pull REDCap version and timestamps for system PHP files; compare to vendor manifest. 2. Contain: isolate host from network, snapshot disk + memory, revoke all REDCap-stored credentials (login table + service accounts), force-reset domain credentials that have ever logged into REDCap admin. 3. Hunt: pivot on the same SHA256s across the fleet, search DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound to 23.169.65.49 (24-month lookback), and audit Google Workspace content compliance + delegation rules for any added since the earliest INFINITERED write date.

Outbound connection to UNC6508 C2 IP 23.169.65.49 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host in the estate beaconing to the UNC6508 C2 IP published by GTIG. INFINITERED takes commands via HTTP cookies on every page load, so the originating process will almost always be a web stack (php-fpm, httpd, nginx) on a REDCap server — that combo is the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Article and pre-extracted IOC name 23.169.65.49 as the UNC6508 C2. Connection from any internal host is high-confidence; from a public-facing REDCap server it is conclusive. CloudWatch left empty because endpoint/VPC-flow telemetry for this campaign is not naturally a CloudTrail signal. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1102
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel platform validating the IOC by reaching out
  • Security researcher sandbox detonating INFINITERED
  • Vulnerability scanner port-knocking the entire IPv4 space (Shodan-style)
  • SOC tabletop or purple-team replaying GTIG IOCs against the estate
  • Stale legacy NAT route still pointing at the (now sinkholed) IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe","CSFalconService.exe","vulnerability-scanner.exe")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the initiating process and host role. If the host is a REDCap server and the process is php-fpm/httpd/w3wp, treat as INFINITERED active beacon. Pull last 90 days of conn attempts and DNS to the same /24. 2. Contain: block 23.169.65.49 at perimeter + EDR network-isolate the host. Capture full memory before reboot. Revoke domain admin and any service-account credentials reachable from the host. 3. Hunt: scan fleet for the seven INFINITERED SHA256s, audit Google Workspace content compliance + forwarding rules created since the earliest beacon, and pivot on `userIdentity` of the domain admin account in Workspace Admin Audit logs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteIP == "23.169.65.49"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, LocalIP, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d) | where DestinationIP == "23.169.65.49" | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction),
  (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d) | where DstIpAddr == "23.169.65.49" | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Google Workspace content compliance rule containing UNC6508 espionage keywords AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation or modification of Gmail content-compliance / mail-routing rules whose keyword list includes the UNC6508 collection priorities — most distinctively the misspelled token 'Patroit' and the disease term 'chikungunya' that GTIG flagged as unique to this rule. This is the actual exfiltration mechanism described in the article. Rationale: GTIG specifically flagged the misspelled keyword 'Patroit' and the unusual term 'chikungunya' in the rule. Either string in a newly-created content-compliance rule is essentially deterministic for UNC6508. Sentinel/Datadog/Falcon/CloudWatch left empty: Google Workspace admin audit logs do not naturally live in those platforms without a custom connector, and a half-correct query would be misleading. Cross-checked against: • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1114/002/
ATT&CKT1114.002 T1098.002 T1020
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate research-compliance rule flagging 'chikungunya' for a public-health institution
  • Red-team or purple-team exercise replaying GTIG IOCs
  • Admin building a regex test that includes the misspelled 'Patroit' string from a news article
  • DLP policy author copy-pasting the keyword list into a test rule
  • Workspace migration tool re-importing a previously-attacker-created rule from backup
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !in~ ("compliance-admin@yourorg.com","dlp-test-svc@yourorg.com")
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full rule body, the admin/service account that created it, source IP, and `IsAdminOperation`. Confirm whether the rule has a BCC/forward action and where to. 2. Contain: delete the rule, suspend the creating admin account, rotate its credentials, revoke OAuth tokens, and force re-auth across all Workspace admins with phishing-resistant MFA. Block the attacker Gmail destination at gateway. 3. Hunt: enumerate all content-compliance, default-routing, and per-user filter rules in the domain for any external-BCC/forward; pivot on every mailbox the rule could have matched and run a content search for the keyword list; check IdentityLogonEvents for the admin in the 30 days prior.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Workspace","Google Apps","Gmail","Google")
| where ActionType has_any ("CREATE_GMAIL_SETTING","CHANGE_GMAIL_SETTING","CREATE_APPLICATION_SETTING","CHANGE_APPLICATION_SETTING","content_compliance_rule_created","CREATE_FILTER")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("Patroit","chikungunya","uncrewed","offensive cyber","geo-strategic","military strategy","advanced technology")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, IsAdminOperation, ActionType, ObjectName, Raw
| order by Timestamp desc

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Workspace","Google Apps","Gmail","Google")
| where ActionType has_any ("CREATE_GMAIL_SETTING","CHANGE_GMAIL_SETTING","CREATE_APPLICATION_SETTING","CHANGE_APPLICATION_SETTING","content_compliance_rule_created","CREATE_FILTER")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("Patroit","chikungunya","uncrewed","offensive cyber","geo-strategic","military strategy","advanced technology")
| project TimeGenerated, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, IsAdminOperation, ActionType, ObjectName, Raw
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Change where Change.action=created AND (Change.object_category=email_rule OR Change.object_category=workspace_policy OR Change.object_category=mail_routing) by Change.user Change.src Change.object Change.command Change.result | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)` | eval keyword_match=if(match(lower(command), "patroit|chikungunya|uncrewed|geo-strategic|offensive cyber|military strategy|advanced technology"), 1, 0) | where keyword_match=1 | table _time user src object command
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change where Change.action=created AND (Change.object_category=email_rule OR Change.object_category=workspace_policy OR Change.object_category=mail_routing) by Change.user Change.src Change.object Change.command Change.result | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)` | eval keyword_match=if(match(lower(command), "patroit|chikungunya|uncrewed|geo-strategic|offensive cyber|military strategy|advanced technology"), 1, 0) | where keyword_match=1 | table _time user src object command
Google Workspace mail rule with BCC or forward to external personal mail provider AIActions on Objectives High
Detects creation of any Gmail content-compliance, routing, or per-user filter rule that BCCs or forwards messages to an address at a free webmail provider (Gmail, Outlook, ProtonMail, Yahoo). UNC6508 exfiltrated to an attacker-controlled Gmail address using exactly this pattern; legitimate internal routing almost never targets a personal-mail domain. Rationale: Article: UNC6508 BCC'd matching mail to an attacker-controlled Gmail address via content compliance rules. Combining the rule-mutation action with an external personal-mail destination keeps this targeted while preserving the exact technique. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1114/003/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence
ATT&CKT1114.003 T1098.002
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee forwarding own mail to personal Gmail (legit but policy-violating)
  • M&A transition period auto-forwarding to acquired-company personal accounts
  • DLP product creating a quarantine route that touches a personal mailbox sink
  • Helpdesk creating a temporary mail-forward for a departing user
  • Workspace migration tool replaying old forwarding configuration
Suppression filter
| where not (AccountDisplayName has_any ("hr-offboard@","dlp-quarantine@") and IsAdminOperation == false)
Response runbook
1. Triage: inspect the rule scope (org-wide vs. single user), the matching condition, and the destination address. Org-wide content compliance with external-personal BCC is always actionable. 2. Contain: delete the rule, suspend the creating account, rotate credentials and revoke OAuth grants. Add the destination address to mail-gateway block. 3. Hunt: list every rule across the domain with `Add forwarding address` or BCC compliance action in the past 24 months; cross-check `super_admin` rights changes via AdminLog; enrich destination addresses against threat intel.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Workspace","Google Apps","Gmail")
| where ActionType has_any ("CREATE_GMAIL_SETTING","CHANGE_GMAIL_SETTING","CREATE_APPLICATION_SETTING","CHANGE_APPLICATION_SETTING","CREATE_FILTER","ADD_FORWARDING_ADDRESS","UPDATE_FORWARDING_ADDRESS")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw matches regex @"(?i)bcc|forward|content_compliance|add_forwarding_address"
| where Raw matches regex @"(?i)@(gmail|outlook|hotmail|yahoo|protonmail|proton\.me|yandex|163|qq)\.(com|me)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, CountryCode, IsAdminOperation, ActionType, ObjectName, Raw
| order by Timestamp desc

CloudAppEvents

| where ActionType has_any ("CREATE_GMAIL_SETTING","CHANGE_GMAIL_SETTING","CREATE_APPLICATION_SETTING","CHANGE_APPLICATION_SETTING","CREATE_FILTER","ADD_FORWARDING_ADDRESS","UPDATE_FORWARDING_ADDRESS")

title: Google Workspace Mail Rule Forwarding to External Personal Mail Provider
id: 5f1d8c2a-3b6e-4a9c-9d7f-2e8b4a1c6f9e
description: Detects creation of a Gmail content-compliance, routing, or per-user filter rule that BCCs or forwards messages to a free-webmail domain — the exfiltration mechanism used by UNC6508.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/chinese-hackers-abused-google-workspace.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1114.003
  - attack.t1098.002
  - attack.collection
logsource:
  product: google_workspace
  service: admin
detection:
  selection_action:
    eventName:
      - 'CREATE_GMAIL_SETTING'
      - 'CHANGE_GMAIL_SETTING'
      - 'CREATE_APPLICATION_SETTING'
      - 'CHANGE_APPLICATION_SETTING'
      - 'CREATE_FILTER'
      - 'ADD_FORWARDING_ADDRESS'
  selection_destination:
    parameters|contains:
      - '@gmail.com'
      - '@outlook.com'
      - '@hotmail.com'
      - '@yahoo.com'
      - '@protonmail.com'
      - '@proton.me'
      - '@yandex.com'
      - '@163.com'
      - '@qq.com'
  condition: selection_action and selection_destination
level: high
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Change where Change.action=created AND (Change.object_category=email_rule OR Change.object_category=mail_routing OR Change.object_category=email_forwarding) by Change.user Change.src Change.object Change.command | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)` | eval has_bcc_or_fwd=if(match(lower(command), "bcc|forward|content_compliance|add_forwarding_address"), 1, 0) | eval external_personal=if(match(lower(command), "@gmail\.com|@outlook\.com|@hotmail\.com|@yahoo\.com|@protonmail\.com|@proton\.me|@yandex\.com|@163\.com|@qq\.com"), 1, 0) | where has_bcc_or_fwd=1 AND external_personal=1 | table _time user src object command
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change where Change.action=created AND (Change.object_category=email_rule OR Change.object_category=mail_routing OR Change.object_category=email_forwarding) by Change.user Change.src Change.object Change.command | `drop_dm_object_name(Change)` | eval has_bcc_or_fwd=if(match(lower(command), "bcc|forward|content_compliance|add_forwarding_address"), 1, 0) | eval external_personal=if(match(lower(command), "@gmail\.com|@outlook\.com|@hotmail\.com|@yahoo\.com|@protonmail\.com|@proton\.me|@yandex\.com|@163\.com|@qq\.com"), 1, 0) | where has_bcc_or_fwd=1 AND external_personal=1 | table _time user src object command
Google Workspace mailbox delegation grant to non-corporate principal AIInstallation Medium
Detects grants of full mailbox delegation, SendOnBehalfOf, or impersonation rights to a principal that is not in the corporate domain or to a recently-created account. UNC6508 reached domain-admin and could equally have used delegation as a persistence mechanism on the mail side; either way, off-domain delegation is a known APT post-compromise pattern. Rationale: Reviewer feedback item #2: GWS rule abuse commonly couples with delegation grants for persistence; article describes domain-admin level mailbox theft and mentions the broader Workspace 'rules' abuse pattern. Filtering to free-webmail delegates keeps signal high. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/002/
ATT&CKT1098.002 T1098.004
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EA delegating an exec mailbox to a personal account during travel
  • Migration tool granting temporary delegation to a service account
  • Outsourced executive-assistant agency on Gmail (Workspace) tenancy mismatch
  • Workspace tenant split during demerger temporarily exposing cross-tenant delegations
  • Helpdesk granting a break-glass delegation to a contractor
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !in~ ("migration-svc@yourorg.com","workspace-bot@yourorg.com")
Response runbook
1. Triage: confirm the granting admin, source IP/geo, and target mailbox; check if granting admin has been involved in other recent rule/permission changes. 2. Contain: revoke the delegation, suspend the granting account if not previously authorised, rotate its credentials, revoke OAuth tokens, enforce phishing-resistant MFA on all admins. 3. Hunt: enumerate every external-domain delegation across the tenant in the past 24 months; pivot on the granting account for any super-admin role assignments; check IdentityLogonEvents for the granting admin in the prior 7 days for impossible-travel.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Workspace","Google Apps","Gmail")
| where ActionType has_any ("CHANGE_MAIL_DELEGATION","CREATE_MAIL_DELEGATION","ADD_MAIL_DELEGATION","GRANT_DELEGATED_MAILBOX_ACCESS","CHANGE_USER_MAILBOX_DELEGATE","AUTHORIZE_DELEGATE_USER")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| extend Delegate = extract(@"(?i)([A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,})", 1, Raw)
| where Delegate matches regex @"(?i)@(gmail|outlook|hotmail|yahoo|protonmail|proton\.me|yandex|163|qq)\.(com|me)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, CountryCode, IsAdminOperation, ActionType, ObjectName, Delegate, Raw
| order by Timestamp desc

| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)

Google Workspace admin or service account reading 10+ distinct mailboxes within 1 hour AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a single Workspace account opening, exporting, or modifying settings on 10 or more distinct user mailboxes within a one-hour window — the access pattern an attacker uses after reaching domain-admin to stage rule creation or bulk collection across the high-value mailbox set described in the article (research and defense email). Rationale: Reviewer feedback item #5 + article's emphasis that UNC6508 reached domain-admin to deploy rules across multiple high-value mailboxes. A single principal touching 10+ mailboxes within 1h is a robust fan-out indicator regardless of which specific Workspace API call is used. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/004/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1114/002/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1114.002 T1530
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • eDiscovery / Vault investigation legitimately spanning many custodians
  • Workspace migration tool walking the user list
  • Backup product enumerating mailboxes nightly
  • Compliance officer doing a keyword search across the tenant
  • Helpdesk batch operation (e.g. updating signatures across HR group)
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !in~ ("vault-discovery@yourorg.com","backup-svc@yourorg.com","workspace-migration@yourorg.com")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the principal (admin vs service account), source IP/geo, action mix, and whether mailbox touches preceded any new rule/delegation. Compare to a 30-day baseline for the same principal. 2. Contain: if pattern is unexpected, suspend the account, rotate credentials, revoke OAuth + reset session cookies, force phishing-resistant MFA, and quarantine any rules/delegations created in the same window. 3. Hunt: enumerate every rule, delegation, and forwarding address created against the touched mailboxes in the window; check IdentityLogonEvents for the principal in the prior 14 days; pivot the source IP across CloudAppEvents and SigninLogs.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Workspace","Google Apps","Gmail")
| where ActionType has_any ("email_log_search","mailbox_access","CHANGE_GMAIL_SETTING","CREATE_GMAIL_SETTING","VAULT_SEARCH","MAILBOX_ACCESS","AccessMailbox")
| summarize Mailboxes = dcount(ObjectName), SampleActions = make_set(ActionType, 20), SampleMailboxes = make_set(ObjectName, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Mailboxes >= 10
| order by Mailboxes desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Application has_any ("Google Workspace","Google Apps","Gmail")
| where ActionType has_any ("email_log_search","mailbox_access","CHANGE_GMAIL_SETTING","CREATE_GMAIL_SETTING","VAULT_SEARCH","MAILBOX_ACCESS","AccessMailbox")
| summarize Mailboxes = dcount(ObjectName), SampleActions = make_set(ActionType, 20), SampleMailboxes = make_set(ObjectName, 20), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Mailboxes >= 10
| order by Mailboxes desc
APPLICATION
`google_workspace_audit` (eventName="email_log_search" OR eventName="mailbox_access" OR eventName="CHANGE_GMAIL_SETTING" OR eventName="CREATE_GMAIL_SETTING" OR eventName="VAULT_SEARCH") | bucket _time span=1h | stats dcount(target_user) as mailboxes values(eventName) as actions earliest(_time) as firstSeen latest(_time) as lastSeen by user src_ip _time | where mailboxes >= 10

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

ImFileEvent
