title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ba6b73b0ca0dc7f86b3b397893ac32d729fd53f9df20643288f141f29d020af7", "db65c1b9f9e4cb4d729f45ad4b6fcf3e277caf9eb4c875425dec93fd883f9136", "c1ac43d23f89d41eb4ff131678ab562ab2cfed9aa334b13767ef141d303b0e5b", "8f0158855a656b629ca76ebca565f18bc25563ded34b65d6771632c20edb68ec", "51a57bfc9ed3eb6451c1c289607814d59e1698c666fb97ac5f694c398f23d045", "4efbef69eb3b09bacff892d6a55778d07c418e7f15eba3cf1245e8cdfd8dda0b", "58bb25777e0aa86bcd2125101e0bca4e8732b03d91bd8d2f205b446a2a8d5c86"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] VS Code / Cursor auto-executes script interpreters via .vscode/tasks.json runOn:folderOpen · [LLM] Creation of .vscode/tasks.json or .githooks/pre-commit in a freshly-cloned repository (TaskJacker / Contagious Interview) · [LLM] Installation of UNK_DeadDrop / Axios-secondary malicious npm packages · [LLM] Composer install of compromised Packagist package roberts/leads · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Installation of UNK_DeadDrop / Yeeth-flagged malicious VS Code extensions · [LLM] VBScript loader → CMD → VS Code extension install chain (UNK_DeadDrop Windows pipeline) · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Beaconing to UNK_DeadDrop / Overlord C2 infrastructure (23.137.105.75:5173 and sibling IPs) · [LLM] Malicious Code-extension or VS Code process invoking Microsoft Graph / SharePoint as C2 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
VS Code / Cursor auto-executes script interpreters via .vscode/tasks.json runOn:folderOpen AIDelivery High
Hunts the UNK_DeadDrop / TaskJacker primitive where opening a cloned repo in VS Code or Cursor triggers a tasks.json task with runOptions.runOn=folderOpen, spawning cmd.exe, wscript.exe, powershell.exe or a shell as a child of the editor. This is the article's core no-user-interaction execution trigger. Rationale: Article explicitly names the runOn:folderOpen technique (adopted by Contagious Interview since December 2025) and the TaskJacker variant that drops tasks.json into existing GitHub repos. Editor → shell/script-interpreter is the precise child-of-editor pattern this primitive produces.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate build tasks defined in tasks.json invoking npm/cargo/make via cmd.exe
  • Developers running VS Code integrated terminal commands
  • Extension developers running --extensionDevelopmentPath debug sessions
  • Pre-commit linters or husky hooks invoked through the IDE
  • Power-user keybindings invoking PowerShell tasks
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm run","yarn run","cargo run","dotnet build","make ","tsc ","jest","vitest")) and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--extensionDevelopmentPath")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the child process launched the moment a folder was opened (no preceding terminal interaction) and read the .vscode/tasks.json from the user's workspace to check for runOptions.runOn=folderOpen. 2) Contain: isolate the device in Defender; revoke any cloud / git / cloud-wallet sessions for the user; remove the cloned repository directory and any installed VSIX extensions (code --list-extensions). 3) Hunt: search the user's mailbox for inbound emails containing GitHub links over the last 30 days, pivot on the parent repo URL on GitHub for sibling clones across the org, and search DeviceNetworkEvents for connections to 23.137.105.75:5173 and the other UNK_DeadDrop infrastructure.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","code.exe","cursor.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--extensionDevelopmentPath","--inspect-extensions"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, Hash
title: VS Code or Cursor Spawning Script Interpreter via tasks.json runOn folderOpen
id: 7e6c1e4b-4b56-4a31-8e6e-7d7d22b6f4c1
description: Detects the UNK_DeadDrop / TaskJacker primitive where opening a cloned repository in VS Code or Cursor triggers tasks.json autorun spawning a shell or script interpreter.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/north-korean-hackers-are-turning.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1204.002
  - attack.t1059
  - attack.t1546
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\Code.exe'
      - '\Cursor.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\certutil.exe'
      - '\bitsadmin.exe'

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\Code.exe OR *\\code.exe OR *\\Cursor.exe OR *\\cursor.exe) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe)

| ParentBaseFileName=/^(Code|Cursor)\.exe$/i

Creation of .vscode/tasks.json or .githooks/pre-commit in a freshly-cloned repository (TaskJacker / Contagious Interview) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the worm-like spread vector where git clone produces a .vscode/tasks.json or .githooks/pre-commit file written by git.exe itself, indicating the cloned repository ships an auto-execution primitive before the user opens it in their IDE. Rationale: Article explicitly names both .vscode/tasks.json (TaskJacker) and .githooks/pre-commit (Contagious Interview's shift from hiding code in tasks.json/package.json) as the silent-on-clone execution primitives. Writing these files via git.exe is the moment the worm-like infection enters the host, before any IDE process runs.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal repos that ship a tasks.json with build aliases
  • Husky / lefthook configuring .githooks via post-checkout
  • Repository templates cloned by developers onboarding new projects
  • Open-source projects with legitimate pre-commit linters
  • Developer clones their own repository to a second machine
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the actual tasks.json — look for runOptions.runOn=folderOpen and any command invoking cmd/wscript/curl/powershell. Read pre-commit for shell escapes or curl|bash patterns. 2) Contain: quarantine the cloned directory; mark the originating GitHub URL as a malicious indicator; revoke the user's GitHub PAT and SSH keys (developer creds may already be staged for theft). 3) Hunt: pivot on the GitHub repo URL across the org to find sibling clones; pull EmailEvents for the recruitment lure that delivered the link; check DeviceNetworkEvents for the user's host beaconing to 23.137.105.75:5173 or the listed UNK_DeadDrop domains.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where (FileName == "tasks.json" and FolderPath has @"\.vscode\")
   or (FileName == "pre-commit" and FolderPath has @"\.githooks\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git.exe","git-remote-https.exe","git-remote-http.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where (TargetFileName == "tasks.json" and TargetFilePath has @"\.vscode\")
   or (TargetFileName == "pre-commit" and TargetFilePath has @"\.githooks\")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("git.exe","git-remote-https.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath

Beaconing to UNK_DeadDrop / Overlord C2 infrastructure (23.137.105.75:5173 and sibling IPs) AICommand & Control Medium
Network detection for outbound connections to the article-named UNK_DeadDrop C2 endpoint 23.137.105.75 on TCP/5173 and the related Overlord-framework IPs 170.205.29.83 and 170.205.30.227. Port 5173 is the Vite dev-server default — the actor is reusing it as cover for the HTTP POST exfiltration channel. Rationale: Article explicitly cites 23.137.105[.]75:5173 as the UNK_DeadDrop exfiltration endpoint and the pre-extracted IOC block lists two sibling IPs (170.205.29.83, 170.205.30.227). Port 5173 is unusual for production traffic and is the Vite dev-server default — strong corroboration that the actor blended into developer-tool noise.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanner / proxy validating the IOC list
  • Security research lab reproducing the IOC
  • Misconfigured Vite dev server pointed at a public IP
  • Internal red-team exercise replaying the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process for the connection — Code.exe, Cursor.exe, wscript.exe or a CMD-spawned child is consistent with the UNK_DeadDrop chain. Pull the user, the host, and any cloned repository paths under the user profile. 2) Contain: isolate the device, block the three IPs and port 5173 at the perimeter, revoke any cryptocurrency-wallet sessions, browser-extension wallet seeds, GitHub PATs and cloud creds the developer holds. 3) Hunt: search for sibling hosts connecting to the same /24, look for HTTP POSTs to ports 5173/3000/4173/8080 from non-browser processes, and review the article's domain IOC list (empowerpharmacy.space, nxlog.tech, ondofinance.tech, etc.) for resolution from any host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("23.137.105.75","170.205.29.83","170.205.30.227")
   or (RemoteIP == "23.137.105.75" and RemotePort == 5173)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("23.137.105.75","170.205.29.83","170.205.30.227")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outbound Connection to UNK_DeadDrop Overlord C2 Infrastructure

Installation of UNK_DeadDrop / Yeeth-flagged malicious VS Code extensions AIInstallation High
Detects installation of the three malicious VSIX extensions flagged by Yeeth Security on the official VS Code Marketplace (ByteBinTools jupyter-powerdev, ToolCraft jupyter-powertools, OLDev markdown-mode-devtools) via the code.cmd / cursor CLI --install-extension flag or VSIX drop into the user's extensions folder. Rationale: Article and Yeeth Security explicitly name three full VSIX filenames and publisher slugs. These strings have no benign use and the marketplace identifiers are stable across the install path — extension install via CLI argument OR a write into the user's .vscode/extensions/ subdirectory both yield a clean true-positive.
ATT&CKT1176 T1505 T1195
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher pulling the VSIX for analysis
  • SOC analyst running detection-validation against the IOC list
  • Sandbox reproducing the attack
Response runbook
1) Triage: list installed extensions via `code --list-extensions` and confirm the publisher/version matches; pull the VSIX contents and the publisher's marketplace page (extensions phone home to SharePoint via Microsoft Graph API per Yeeth). 2) Contain: uninstall the extension, isolate the host, revoke any Microsoft 365 / SharePoint sessions for the user (the C2 channel rides Graph), block the SharePoint sites identified during forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot on user's SharePoint activity in OfficeActivity for the prior 30 days for unexpected file uploads/downloads, check other devs in the org that may have installed the same marketplace items, and search EmailEvents for the lure that recommended the extension.
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--install-extension","install-extension")
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ByteBinTools.jupyter-powerdev","ToolCraft.jupyter-powertools","OLDev.markdown-mode-devtools","jupyter-powerdev-2026.6.8.vsix","jupyter-powertools-3.21.0.vsix","markdown-mode-devtools-2.1.0.vsix")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName has_any ("jupyter-powerdev","jupyter-powertools","markdown-mode-devtools","ByteBinTools","ToolCraft.jupyter","OLDev.markdown")
  | where FolderPath has_any (@"\.vscode\extensions\",@"\.cursor\extensions\")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName )
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ByteBinTools.jupyter-powerdev","ToolCraft.jupyter-powertools","OLDev.markdown-mode-devtools","jupyter-powerdev-2026.6.8.vsix","jupyter-powertools-3.21.0.vsix","markdown-mode-devtools-2.1.0.vsix")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Malicious Code-extension or VS Code process invoking Microsoft Graph / SharePoint as C2 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the Yeeth-Security backdoor pattern where the JavaScript layer inside a malicious VS Code extension uses Microsoft Graph API and SharePoint as its command-queue / exfiltration channel. Detection fires when the VS Code helper / extension-host process makes outbound calls to graph.microsoft.com or *.sharepoint.com that don't match the canonical Visual Studio / GitHub Copilot / settings-sync paths. Rationale: Article: 'A JavaScript layer that handles all command-and-control (C2) communication via Microsoft Graph API and SharePoint' for the three Yeeth-flagged extensions. The detection scopes specifically to processes that live inside the VS Code / Cursor extension-host runtime, and excludes the canonical Microsoft-shipped settings-sync and Copilot extensions to keep noise down.
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft-published settings-sync extension legitimately syncing
  • GitHub Copilot extension calling Graph for telemetry
  • Legitimate third-party SharePoint / OneDrive integrations
  • Custom internal extension that uses Graph for valid work
  • Live Share extension presence calls
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("GitHub.copilot","ms-vscode.azure-account","ms-vscode.vscode-settings-sync"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the running extension list (`code --list-extensions --show-versions`) and cross-reference against the three Yeeth IOCs; if no match, examine the actual extension manifest at %USERPROFILE%\.vscode\extensions\ for the Graph/SharePoint endpoint URLs. 2) Contain: uninstall the implicated extension, revoke the user's M365 refresh tokens via Entra ID, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pull OfficeActivity for SharePoint file uploads/downloads from the user during the same window — the article calls out 'pwd, ls, cd, cat' style host_action commands and file upload/download as the abuse pattern.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","node.exe","electron.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("graph.microsoft.com",".sharepoint.com")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\.vscode\extensions\",@"\.cursor\extensions\",@"\AppData\Local\Programs\Microsoft VS Code\",@"\Cursor\")
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ms-vscode.vscode-settings-sync","GitHub.copilot","ms-vscode-remote"))
| summarize Count=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine), SampleUrl=any(RemoteUrl) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Count desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("graph.microsoft.com",".sharepoint.com")
| where SrcHostname has_any ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","node.exe") or HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("VSCode","Cursor","node")
| summarize Count=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), SampleUrl=any(Url) by SrcHostname, SrcUsername, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by Count desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\Code.exe OR *\\Cursor.exe OR *\\node.exe OR *\\electron.exe) @DestinationHostname:(*graph.microsoft.com* OR *.sharepoint.com*) -@CommandLine:(*GitHub.copilot* OR *ms-vscode.vscode-settings-sync*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(Code|Cursor|node|electron)\.exe$/i
| DomainName=/(graph\.microsoft\.com|\.sharepoint\.com)$/i
| NOT (CommandLine=/GitHub\.copilot|ms-vscode\.vscode-settings-sync/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest) as dest from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_url="*graph.microsoft.com*" OR All_Traffic.dest_url="*.sharepoint.com*") AND All_Traffic.app IN ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","node.exe") by host All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest_url
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.dest) as dest from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest_url="*graph.microsoft.com*" OR All_Traffic.dest_url="*.sharepoint.com*") AND All_Traffic.app IN ("Code.exe","Cursor.exe","node.exe") by host All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest_url
Installation of UNK_DeadDrop / Axios-secondary malicious npm packages AIDelivery High
Detects the installation or registry fetch of the three named-and-shamed npm packages used as the Axios supply-chain follow-up: redeem-onchain-sdk@1.0.7, nicegui@0.1.4 and period-newline@0.1.0. Each ships an info-stealer payload reachable from any project that pulls them as a dependency. Rationale: Article explicitly names three npm package@version strings. 'period-newline' is a particularly unique slug; combined with the version constraints these have a near-zero benign collision rate. Detection covers both the install command line and the resulting node_modules directory write.
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher inspecting the IOC packages
  • Internal SCA scanner mirroring the registry index
  • Sandbox reproducing the attack chain
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump package-lock.json / yarn.lock / pnpm-lock.yaml from the workspace and confirm the version; identify upstream repos that listed the package as a dependency (article notes these were placed in 'cryptocurrency trading bot' GitHub repos). 2) Contain: uninstall the package, scrub node_modules and lock files, rotate any credentials accessible from the dev machine (the secondary payload is an infostealer), isolate the host. 3) Hunt: search GitHub org-wide for any repo that referenced these packages and notify owners; pivot on the dev's outbound DNS and HTTP for the article's C2 IOC list — secondary payloads ship to different infrastructure per OpenSourceMalware.
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.cmd","npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd") or FileName in~ ("npm.cmd","npm.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd")
  | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("redeem-onchain-sdk","period-newline","nicegui@0.1.4")
     or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("redeem-onchain-sdk","period-newline","nicegui@0.1.4")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\redeem-onchain-sdk",@"\node_modules\nicegui",@"\node_modules\period-newline")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName )
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("npm.cmd","npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.cmd","pnpm.cmd")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("redeem-onchain-sdk","period-newline","nicegui@0.1.4")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Composer install of compromised Packagist package roberts/leads AIDelivery High
Detects PHP developers pulling the Contagious Interview-compromised Packagist package roberts/leads via composer require / install / update. The package contains a JavaScript loader that fetches a next-stage payload from blockchain RPC infrastructure and ultimately deploys a DEV#POPPER RAT variant. Rationale: Article explicitly names 'roberts/leads' as the compromised Packagist package. The slug is unique enough to be a high-fidelity string match, and the vendor/roberts/leads filesystem path confirms a real install (vs. just a string mention in logs).
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Detection validation
  • Researcher inspecting the package
  • Internal mirror caching the package
Response runbook
1) Triage: read composer.lock and confirm the installed version; pull the vendor/roberts/leads contents — article notes the JS loader reaches blockchain/RPC infrastructure to fetch decryption keys. 2) Contain: composer remove the package, purge vendor/, isolate the host, rotate developer credentials and SSH keys (DEV#POPPER variant per Trend Micro is credential-theft focused). 3) Hunt: scan the org's PHP repos for the package via Dependabot or grep over composer.json; check outbound DNS for the actor's domain IOCs (empowerpharmacy.space, nxlog.tech, etc.) and search the dev's recent git push history for tampered commits (article explicitly calls out the actor injecting code into the victim's own repos).
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where (FileName in~ ("composer.phar","composer.bat","php.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("composer.phar","composer.bat","php.exe"))
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "roberts/leads" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "roberts/leads"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FolderPath has @"\vendor\roberts\leads"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName )
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("composer.phar","composer.bat","php.exe") or ParentProcessName has_any ("composer.phar","composer.bat","php.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "roberts/leads" or ParentProcessCommandLine has "roberts/leads"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

VBScript loader → CMD → VS Code extension install chain (UNK_DeadDrop Windows pipeline) AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact Windows UNK_DeadDrop kill chain documented by Proofpoint: a VBScript loader is dropped from a cloned GitHub repo, wscript.exe runs the loader which executes a CMD file, the CMD file installs the malicious VSIX extension. Detection chains wscript→cmd→code.cmd with extension-install context. Rationale: Article spells out the Windows pipeline verbatim: 'the Windows attack chain ... relies on the VBScript payload to run a CMD file, which then installs the extension.' This UC encodes the parent=wscript with a VBS argument → cmd / code.cmd grandparent pivot, optionally chained with --install-extension to bind it to the VSIX install step.
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1059.003 T1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate VBS-based installer launching cmd
  • Build systems that wrap setup logic in WSH
  • Enterprise MDM bootstrap scripts
  • Developer's own VBS automation for local dev
  • VS Code remote-tunnel installer using VBS shims (rare)
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the .vbs / .wsf file referenced in the parent command line and the .cmd file it spawns; both are dropped from the cloned GitHub repo per Proofpoint. Inspect for the article's known VSIX strings and the 23.137.105.75:5173 callback. 2) Contain: isolate the host, uninstall the dropped VSIX, kill the wscript / cmd / Code process tree, revoke the user's cloud-wallet sessions. 3) Hunt: pivot DeviceFileEvents on the .vbs filename to find sibling drops org-wide and across the user's other devices; check git command history for the originating clone URL and flag it as malicious in the org's GitHub tenant.
let WScriptParent = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
  | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "wscript.exe"
  | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (".vbs",".vbe",".wsf")
  | where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","code.cmd","code.exe","cursor.cmd","cursor.exe")
  | project CmdTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, VBSCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, CmdImage=FileName, CmdFullCmd=ProcessCommandLine, ChainProcessId=ProcessId;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName =~ "code.cmd" or FileName =~ "code.exe" or FileName =~ "cursor.cmd")
   and ProcessCommandLine has "--install-extension"
| join kind=inner WScriptParent on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (CmdTime .. CmdTime + 5m)
| project CmdTime, InstallTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, VBSCmd, CmdFullCmd, InstallCmd=ProcessCommandLine
| order by CmdTime desc
let WScriptParent = ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where ParentProcessName has "wscript.exe"
  | where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any (".vbs",".vbe",".wsf")
  | where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","code.cmd","code.exe","cursor.cmd")
  | project CmdTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, VBSCmd=ParentProcessCommandLine, CmdImage=ActingProcessName, CmdFullCmd=ActingProcessCommandLine;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("code.cmd","code.exe","cursor.cmd") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--install-extension"
| join kind=inner WScriptParent on DvcHostname, ActorUsername
| where TimeGenerated between (CmdTime .. CmdTime + 5m)
| project CmdTime, InstallTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, VBSCmd, CmdFullCmd, InstallCmd=ActingProcessCommandLine
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\code.cmd OR *\\Code.exe OR *\\cursor.cmd) @ParentCommandLine:(*.vbs* OR *.vbe* OR *.wsf*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentBaseFileName=/wscript\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|code(\.cmd)?|cursor(\.cmd)?)\.exe$/i
| ParentCommandLine=/\.(vbs|vbe|wsf)\b/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentCommandLine, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="wscript.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","code.cmd","code.exe","cursor.cmd") by host Processes.user Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where lastTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="wscript.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","code.cmd","code.exe","cursor.cmd") by host Processes.user Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where lastTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d")
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents

          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

let BadHashes = dynamic(["35813f4401d3ad77b618275473a556eb47bfa6f4b7439dd8943b19f81aa7252e", "c935808147f0236c81483d7bbeda4b9d602f3595d5d4057f8115d39e222d1c4b", "4c0d9b802c075be79e9edb52d88f8dd72e6904f5c58267213745818470945c78", "62761f38ed194c59abe15c49f09f0ebc431ac852c965180c9327ed84d3a454fb", "d3ebce2f05fe91a8260e87fd11a6ea17c156703d081b3f91d9bbe5fd6aeedc10", "91b9381d19b2e6a2db5cc0307167979b502731cb3fb50da684479e9ed35261aa", "6cf9f7b2aa456a0b438600588df869b38d8007e28f01fa96022f9d8059f120b0", "2812e0847d472cb8870c94f463331dbe53b84135132b9bf5f6d84c2382be628f", "52886aab179f26421678ff23af1b0fabf0a17ffbb534369cdbbac8008cbed8e7", "d5e9288693aa745dc89368deac677e7ea1ec81e663283af30838cdae189b7a7e", "734699773e53d995f20d485eb61261033d9d00b4332b39ca26071bcd60cd352f", "e1bf1b29e6fa3525d7f32f429290a88d6ea2890e61c06574b8ff6372aa5d0667", "a2b9a769df84d9d3a4694bb0252a2c6a5e5f5d1a85a04565362737092bbb3a86", "bb10adac5b0124efedfe71102c1d5638135ec9e1cde8c8cb3353c5ed91bb9f81", "339907b44f161f57ff30819f422c552382ff437b3ae437463b4222cfe86bd943", "808e7154b7af2bc7a4b28d577297c55f77221c355191cbe00f9f1810b6d4a619"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OptinMonster WordPress plugin hacked in CDN supply-chain attack

BleepingComputer
2026-06-15 7 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

WordPress plugins OptinMonster, TrustPulse, and PushEngage have been compromised in a supply-chain attack impacting Awesome Motive-s content distribution network (CDN). [...]

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190
Domainstidio.cc a.omappapi.com a.opmnstr.com a.optnmstr.com a.trstplse.com clientcdn.pushengage.com
IPs84.201.6.54

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] WP admin browser loads poisoned Awesome Motive CDN api.min.js (OptinMonster/TrustPulse/PushEngage)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — OptinMonster WordPress plugin hacked in CDN supply-chain attack
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Backdoor WordPress plugin folder created (Content Delivery Helper / Database Optimizer) · [LLM] Rogue WordPress administrator account created (developer_api1 / dev_xxxxxx pattern)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to Tidio-impersonating exfil host (tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
WP admin browser loads poisoned Awesome Motive CDN api.min.js (OptinMonster/TrustPulse/PushEngage) AIDelivery High
Hunts WordPress administrators whose browsers fetched the trojanized OptinMonster/TrustPulse/PushEngage JS from Awesome Motive's CDN during the June 12-13 2026 compromise window. The exact host+path are public IOCs from Sansec / Awesome Motive's advisory, so any hit inside the window is a near-certain admin-token theft event. Rationale: Uses the four exact CDN host+path strings published by Awesome Motive plus the PushEngage CDN host, all from the article. Window-bounded to the published compromise interval (22:17 UTC Fri → 19:02 UTC Sat) — outside that window these URLs are legitimate plugin assets, inside it every fetch is poisoned.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1189 T1539
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate OptinMonster/TrustPulse/PushEngage plugin loads outside the June 12-13 2026 window (filter strictly excludes these via window bound)
  • Security researcher/IR replay of pcaps containing the malicious URLs after the fact
  • Sandbox detonation systems rendering archived copies of victim sites
  • DAST/web crawler tooling re-fetching cached IOC lists for validation
Suppression filter
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-06-12T22:17:00Z) .. datetime(2026-06-13T19:02:00Z))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: For each hit, pull the device's full DeviceProcessEvents within 5 min of the load — look for browser-spawned tools or session-cookie export. Identify whether the user is/was a WordPress administrator on any company-managed site. 2) CONTAIN: Force-reset that user's WordPress admin credentials, API keys, and security salts across every WP site they admin; rotate session cookies. Have them re-audit user list for 'developer_api1' / 'dev_xxxxxx' admins (see UC4). 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC2 (tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54 egress from the same host or WP servers) and UC3 (backdoor plugin folder under wp-content/plugins/ on their managed sites).

Outbound C2 to Tidio-impersonating exfil host (tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54) AICommand & Control Medium
Catches the backdoor's exfil/command channel — the rogue plugin beacons stolen WordPress data to a tidio.cc lookalike of the legitimate Tidio chat service, and Sansec attributes IP 84.201.6.54 to the operation. Either indicator is a definitive post-compromise signal. Rationale: tidio.cc is the article-published Tidio-lookalike C2 host (legit Tidio is tidio.com — the .cc TLD is the typosquat); 84.201.6.54 is the article's IP IOC. Excluding tidio.com avoids the obvious FP. Both indicators are unique to this operation per the article so any hit is high-fidelity.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution Network_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IR/researcher manually browsing or curl-ing the IOC for validation (filterable by source process)
  • Threat-intel platforms auto-validating the IOC (e.g. URLScan, VirusTotal re-test) — typically not on production endpoints
  • Internal sandbox detonation of captured samples reaching out
  • Legitimate Tidio integration accidentally mistyping the TLD — unlikely but possible during config (would be a one-off, not persistent)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify whether the hit came from a WordPress server, an admin workstation browser, or a generic endpoint. Pull the initiating process and its parent — backdoor activity from `php-fpm`, `apache2`, or `nginx` workers is near-certain compromise. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host. For WP servers, halt the web service and snapshot `wp-content/plugins/` and the wp_users / wp_usermeta tables before any cleanup. Sinkhole or block tidio.cc + 84.201.6.54 at egress. 3) HUNT: Sweep all managed WP sites for the backdoor plugin folders (UC3) and rogue admin accounts (UC4). Rotate every credential/API key/salt the affected sites hold per Awesome Motive's advisory.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "tidio.cc" or RemoteIP == "84.201.6.54"
| where not(RemoteUrl has "tidio.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DnsQuery has "tidio.cc"
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Indicator=DnsQuery, IndicatorType="DNS"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where DestinationIP == "84.201.6.54" or RequestURL has "tidio.cc"
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr=SourceIP, SrcHostname=SourceHostName, SrcUsername=SourceUserName, Indicator=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationIP), IndicatorType="NET")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Backdoor WordPress plugin folder created (Content Delivery Helper / Database Optimizer) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the rogue plugin directories that Sansec observed the operator deploying with byte-identical logic under rotating disguises — currently `content-delivery-helper` (v2.7.1) and `database-optimizer` (v2.9.4). High-fidelity because these specific names under `wp-content/plugins/` are not the legitimate plugins they impersonate. Rationale: Both plugin slugs are direct quotes from Sansec via the article. Anchoring on the `wp-content/plugins/` parent path rules out unrelated repos that may use similar names. Sansec notes the operator rotates the disguise — these are the two currently observed; the slug list should be appended to as new aliases emerge.
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1543 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate plugin developer locally creating a dev plugin coincidentally named 'database-optimizer' — extremely unlikely on production WP hosts, more plausible on dev workstations
  • Backup/restore operations writing an archived copy of the same backdoor (still a hit — confirms compromise of the source backup)
  • Threat-intel sandbox unpacking the sample
  • Plugin migration tools renaming legitimate Awesome Motive plugins (not the case for these names — they are not Awesome Motive plugin slugs)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: List the full file tree under each hit directory and hash every file. The article identifies a 'WPM File Manager & Shell' web shell + arbitrary PHP exec inside — those PHP files are the smoking gun. Capture before deletion. 2) CONTAIN: Take the WordPress site offline. Remove the plugin directory, then audit `wp_options` (active_plugins), `wp_users`, and `wp_usermeta` for rogue admins (UC4). Force-reset WP salts, DB password, all admin passwords, and any API keys (the attacker had full PHP exec — assume all secrets readable from wp-config.php were stolen). 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC2 (tidio.cc / 84.201.6.54 egress from this host's IP) and UC1 (which admin browser loaded the poisoned CDN JS — that's the initial token-theft vector).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "wp-content/plugins/"
| where FolderPath has_any ("content-delivery-helper","database-optimizer")
   or FileName has_any ("content-delivery-helper","database-optimizer")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RequestAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has "wp-content/plugins/"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("content-delivery-helper","database-optimizer")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
